pos: n. (Thuringian city and university; where Luther took his degrees, entered the Augustinian cloister in 1505, and was ordained)
etymology: From Old High German Erphesfurt, the ford of the Erpf; Latin Erfordia.
biblical_def: Erfurt was the making of Martin Luther and nearly the undoing of him. He matriculated in its university in 1501, took his master's degree there, and in July 1505, after the thunderstorm near Stotternheim, entered the Augustinian cloister in the city against his father's will. There he kept the rule with a severity his brethren remembered, confessed until his confessor lost patience, and found that the harder he laboured the less peace he had; the law, applied honestly to himself, gave him knowledge of sin and no remedy for it. The remedy came later at Wittenberg, out of the Psalms and Romans, but the question came from Erfurt. The dictionary records the city because this is where the Reformation's central question was framed by a man who had taken the old answer as far as it would go. “Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin” (Rom 3:20) is the whole report of those cloister years, and the law's true office follows: it “was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ” (Gal 3:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines law in Scripture as the revealed will of God and the rule of moral conduct, justification as the act of free grace by which God pardons the sinner and accepts him as righteous, and a monastery as a convent of monks.
webster_full: LAW, n. In Scripture, the Mosaic institutions, or the revealed will of God; the rule of moral conduct.
JUSTIFICA'TION, n. In theology, remission of sin and absolution from guilt and punishment; or an act of free grace by which God pardons the sinner and accepts him as righteous.
MON'ASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement; a convent of monks.
SCHOOLMASTER, n. The man who presides over and teaches a school; a teacher, instructor, preceptor.
scriptures: Rom 3:20
Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.
Gal 3:24
Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.
Rom 1:17
For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith.
Hab 2:4
Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.
corruption_summary: Luther's university and Augustinian cloister, where the law gave him knowledge of sin and no peace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern habit of easing a troubled conscience by lowering the standard — telling the man who cannot keep the law that the law was never meant so strictly. Erfurt tried the opposite and is worth more: Luther took the law at full weight, failed, and was driven to look elsewhere for righteousness.

The principle to recover is that the law cannot justify and was never given to justify, and that its failure to justify is part of its usefulness. Scripture is explicit about both halves: “by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin” (Rom 3:20). The office is custodial and preparatory — the law “was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (Gal 3:24). What the cloister could not supply, the gospel reveals: “For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith” (Rom 1:17), citing the prophet: “the just shall live by his faith” (Hab 2:4).
roots_summary: Greek dikaioo (G1344), to declare righteous; Hebrew emunah (H530), faithfulness, faith.
roots_lines: Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, to acquit judicially; Romans 3:20.
Greek epignosis (G1922) — full knowledge, here the knowledge of sin; Romans 3:20.
Greek paidagogos (G3807) — a child-guide, the law's custodial office; Galatians 3:24.
Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness, the standing God gives; Romans 1:17.
Hebrew emunah (H530) — steadfastness, faithfulness, faith; Habakkuk 2:4.

“the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ” (Gal 3:24) — a confessor who lost patience with his penitent.
“the just shall live by his faith” (Hab 2:4) — the question framed at Erfurt and answered at Wittenberg.

pos: n. (Thuringian university founded 1558; stronghold of the strict Lutherans against the Philippist party)
etymology: From Old High German Jani, of uncertain sense, perhaps a word for a river meadow; German Jena.
biblical_def: Jena was founded by the Ernestine Saxons as a counterweight to Wittenberg, which after Luther's death had passed to the milder party gathered round Melanchthon. Matthias Flacius taught at Jena, and from its chairs the strict Lutherans pressed two charges: that the Leipzig Interim had surrendered the gospel under the pretence that vestments and ceremonies were things indifferent, and that the Philippists had conceded a cooperating power to the unregenerate will. On the second point Jena was right and Flacius then overshot it, defining original sin as the very substance of fallen man, which the Formula of Concord had to correct. The dictionary records Jena as a case where the right doctrine was defended with a wrong definition. Scripture leaves the will no cooperating power — “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44) — without making sin the substance of the creature God made.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the will as the faculty by which we determine to do or forbear an action, bondage as involuntary servitude and restraint of liberty by compulsion, and depravity as a vitiated state and corruption of moral principles.
webster_full: WILL, n. That faculty of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action.
BONDAGE, n. Slavery or involuntary servitude; captivity; imprisonment; restraint of a person's liberty by compulsion.
DEPRAV'ITY, n. A vitiated state; corruption of moral principles.
NATURE, n. The essence, essential qualities or attributes of a thing, which constitute it what it is.
scriptures: Rom 7:18
For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
corruption_summary: The Ernestine university of the strict Lutherans, where Flacius defended bound will and then overshot into making sin man's substance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the semi-Pelagian concession that the unregenerate will retains some power to turn toward God and merely needs help — the position Jena was founded to resist, and which returns in every generation under a new name.

The principle to recover is total inability, held without exaggeration. The fallen man wills and cannot perform: “to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not” (Rom 7:18). Coming to Christ requires a divine act prior to the will's motion: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44). The state before grace is death, not weakness — “And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) — and the prophet puts the impossibility as a question: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?” (Jer 13:23).
roots_summary: Greek helko (G1670), to draw; Greek sarx (G4561), flesh as fallen nature.
roots_lines: Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh, human nature as fallen; Romans 7:18.
Greek katergazomai (G2716) — to work out, to accomplish fully; Romans 7:18.
Greek helko (G1670) — to draw, to drag with force; John 6:44.
Greek suzoopoieo (G4806) — to make alive together with; Ephesians 2:5.
Greek nekros (G3498) — dead, without life; Ephesians 2:1.

“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44) — Flacius in the chair and the Interim refused.
“who were dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) — right doctrine defended with a wrong definition.

pos: n. (Wurttemberg university founded 1477; home of Brenz, Jakob Andreae and the Swabian Christology)
etymology: From Old High German Tuwingen, of uncertain sense; German Tubingen.
biblical_def: Tubingen trained the theologians of Wurttemberg and through them shaped Lutheran Christology. Johannes Brenz and Jakob Andreae taught there; Andreae was the chief architect of the Formula of Concord of 1577, and the Swabian doctrine of the communication of attributes — that the human nature of Christ truly receives the divine majesty — was framed in its lecture rooms. Two centuries later the same university housed the most destructive school of historical criticism in Europe, which denied what its own forefathers had defended. The dictionary records Tubingen with both facts in view, because an institution does not keep a confession by inheriting one. The doctrine the first Tubingen defended is the doctrine the dictionary holds: one Person in two natures, truly God and truly man. “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (Joh 1:14), and in that flesh “dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines incarnation as the act of assuming flesh and taking a human body and the nature of man, nature as the essential attributes which constitute a thing what it is, and fulness as the state of being filled so as to leave no part vacant.
webster_full: INCARNA'TION, n. The act of clothing with flesh; the act of assuming flesh, or of taking a human body and the nature of man.
NATURE, n. The essence, essential qualities or attributes of a thing, which constitute it what it is.
FUL'NESS, n. The state of being filled, so as to leave no part vacant; abundance.
FORM, n. A model to be imitated; a prescribed mode or order; a pattern.
scriptures: Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Php 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Heb 2:14

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;
corruption_summary: The Wurttemberg university of Brenz and Andreae, where the Formula of Concord and the Swabian Christology were framed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is the one the later Tubingen school produced: a critical method that treated the incarnation as the church's developing idea rather than an event, and the Gospels as deposits of that idea. The dictionary names that method as what it is, and notes that it grew in the very place that had defended the doctrine it dissolved.

The principle to recover is the Chalcedonian confession, one Person and two natures, united without confusion, change, division or separation. The incarnation is an act and not an idea: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (Joh 1:14). The deity is not diminished by it: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9). The humiliation is real and voluntary — He “took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Php 2:7) — and it was undertaken for a purpose no idea could accomplish: “that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death” (Heb 2:14).
roots_lines: Greek skenoo (G4637) — to pitch a tent, to dwell among; John 1:14.
Greek monogenes (G3439) — only begotten, uniquely of the Father; John 1:14.
Greek pleroma (G4138) — fulness, that which fills completely; Colossians 2:9.
Greek theotes (G2320) — deity, the divine essence itself; Colossians 2:9.
Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty, to make of no reputation; Philippians 2:7.
usage: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (Joh 1:14) — Brenz and Andreae in the Wurttemberg chairs.
“all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9) — the Formula of Concord, 1577.
“took upon him the form of a servant” (Php 2:7) — and the later school that dissolved what the first defended.

pos: n. (Prussian city and university founded 1544; scene of the Osiandrian controversy over justification)
etymology: From German Konigsberg, the king's mountain, named for Ottokar of Bohemia; Latin Regiomontum.
biblical_def: Konigsberg is where the Reformation's central doctrine was nearly lost from the inside. Duke Albert founded the university in 1544 and in 1549 gave a chair to Andreas Osiander, who had served Nuremberg well in the 1520s. Osiander now taught that a man is justified not by the imputed obedience of Christ reckoned to him, but by the essential righteousness of Christ indwelling him — which makes justification a change in the believer rather than a verdict upon him, and so collapses it into sanctification. Prussia was torn for a decade, Osiander died in 1552, and the Formula of Concord settled the matter against him. The dictionary records Konigsberg because the error was committed by a Reformer of real service, which is how such errors usually arrive. Scripture keeps justification forensic, and the verdict falls on a man who has done nothing: “justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to impute as to charge, to attribute, to set to the account of another, to justify in theology as to pardon and clear from guilt, and righteousness as conformity of heart and life to the divine law.
webster_full: IMPUTE, v.t. To charge; to attribute; to set to the account of another.
JUSTIFY, v.t. In theology, to pardon and clear from guilt; to absolve or acquit from guilt and merited punishment.
RIGHTEOUSNESS, n. Purity of heart and rectitude of life; conformity of heart and life to the divine law.
FAITH, n. The assent of the mind to the truth of what God has revealed; a firm and cordial belief.
scriptures: Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
Php 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Rom 5:19
For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
corruption_summary: The Prussian university where Osiander taught justification by indwelling righteousness, and the Formula of Concord answered him.
corruption_paragraphs: Osiandrianism is a live corruption, not a dead one. Wherever justification is presented as the infusion of a new quality rather than the imputation of Christ's obedience, the believer is thrown back on the state of his own heart for his assurance, and the ground of peace with God shifts from a finished verdict to a measurable progress. Rome teaches it as a system; evangelicals reproduce it whenever they make the new life the ground rather than the fruit of acceptance.

The principle to recover is that justification is a judicial act of God, external to the sinner, grounded in Christ's obedience reckoned to him. The object of the verdict is the ungodly as such: “to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5). The exchange is double imputation: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21). Paul will not own any righteousness of his own — “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Php 3:9) — and the ground is another's obedience: “by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19).
roots_summary: Greek logizomai (G3049), to reckon to an account; Greek hupakoe (G5218), obedience.
roots_lines: Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to count to one's account; Romans 4:5.
Greek asebes (G765) — ungodly, the one justified; Romans 4:5.
Greek hamartia (G266) — sin, which He was made for us; 2 Corinthians 5:21.
Greek hupakoe (G5218) — obedience, the ground of the verdict; Romans 5:19.

“that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21) — Prussia torn for a decade.
“by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19) — the Formula of Concord against indwelling righteousness.

pos: n. (Brunswick university founded 1576; the chair of Georg Calixtus and the home of Lutheran syncretism)
etymology: From Old Saxon Helmonstede, Helmo's place; German Helmstedt.
biblical_def: Helmstedt is the university of a proposal the dictionary must decline. Georg Calixtus held its chair of theology for forty years and argued for a reunion of Lutheran, Reformed and Roman Christianity on the basis of the Apostles' Creed and the consensus of the first five centuries, with the later confessional differences treated as matters a church might hold without dividing over. His opponents at Wittenberg named the proposal syncretism, and the ensuing controversy occupied German theology for a generation. The dictionary notes Calixtus's learning and his genuine horror of the wars of religion, and still names his method as error: the doctrines he set aside as secondary include justification by faith alone, on which the whole quarrel with Rome turned. A standard narrowed to the first five centuries is a standard chosen by men. Scripture binds the church to the whole deposit: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines syncretism as the attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance, a pattern as an original or model proposed for imitation, and to consent as to concur in sentiment or act.
webster_full: SYNCRETISM, n. The attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance.
PATTERN, n. An original or model proposed for imitation; the archetype; an exemplar.
CONSENT, v.i. To agree; to yield; to concur in sentiment or act.
AR'TICLE, n. A single clause in a contract, account, system of regulations, treaty, or other writing; a particular item.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness;
Pro 30:6
Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar.
For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:
corruption_summary: The chair of Georg Calixtus, whose reunion on the first five centuries set aside justification by faith alone as secondary.
corruption_paragraphs: Syncretism is a live and growing corruption. In its modern form it does not propose the first five centuries but a shorter list still — a bare theism, a shared ethic, a common spirituality — and it always arrives recommending peace. The cost is always the same: the articles struck off the list are the ones that were contested, and the ones that were contested are the ones that mattered.

The principle to recover is that the standard of the church's unity is the whole revealed word and not a selection from it. The deposit is to be held in the shape it was given: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13). Teaching otherwise is named, not negotiated with: “If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words” (1Ti 6:3). Addition is forbidden — “Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar” (Pro 30:6) — and so, by the same token, is subtraction: “If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book” (Rev 22:18).

roots_lines: Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, a pattern to be kept; 2 Timothy 1:13.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, wholesome, healthy; 2 Timothy 1:13.

Greek proserchomai (G4334) — to come to, to assent to; 1 Timothy 6:3.
Hebrew yasaph (H3254) — to add, to increase upon; Proverbs 30:6.

“If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words” (1Ti 6:3) — the syncretistic controversy with Wittenberg.
“Add thou not unto his words” (Pro 30:6) — a standard narrowed to five centuries is a standard chosen by men.

pos: n. (Hessian university founded 1607; one party in the kenosis controversy with Tubingen over Christ's use of the divine attributes)
etymology: From German Giessen, a pouring or a watercourse, from giessen, to pour.
biblical_def: Giessen gave its name to one side of a controversy that occupied Lutheran theology from 1619 to 1627. Both Giessen and Tubingen held that the incarnate Son possessed the divine attributes in His human nature; they divided over what He did with them in the days of His flesh. The Giessen theologians held that He refrained from using them — a withholding of use; Tubingen held that He used them continually but secretly — a hiding of use. The Saxon decision of 1624 inclined to Giessen, and the matter was left where confessional Lutheranism leaves it. The dictionary records the dispute without adopting either term, because the Reformed answer runs along a different line: the Person acts according to each nature as the work requires, and the humiliation is real without any emptying of deity. “Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power” (Heb 1:3) was true throughout.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines majesty as greatness of appearance and dignity, glory as that in which one may exult and rejoice, and fulness as the state of being filled so as to leave no part vacant.
webster_full: MAJ'ESTY, n. Greatness of appearance; dignity; title of emperors, kings and queens.
GLORY, v.i. To boast; to be proud of; to exult with joy; to rejoice.
FUL'NESS, n. The state of being filled, so as to leave no part vacant; abundance.
NATURE, n. The essence, essential qualities or attributes of a thing, which constitute it what it is.
scriptures: Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
Joh 17:5
And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.
And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.
Col 1:19
For it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell;
corruption_summary: One party in the Lutheran kenosis controversy of 1619 to 1627, over whether Christ withheld or merely hid the use of the divine attributes.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is not either Lutheran position but the nineteenth-century kenotic theology that grew out of the vocabulary: the claim that in the incarnation the Son actually laid aside omniscience and omnipotence, so that His errors in matters of fact could be conceded while His divinity was still professed. That doctrine is used today chiefly to excuse treating the Lord's own testimony to the Scriptures as mistaken.

The principle to recover is that the humiliation of the Son touched His estate and not His essence. The upholding of the universe never ceased: He is the one “upholding all things by the word of his power” (Heb 1:3). The glory He prays to receive again is the glory He had and did not lose: “glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was” (Joh 17:5). The Mediator's authority is declared without reserve — “All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth” (Mat 28:18) — and the Father's good pleasure is that nothing be lacking in Him: “that in him should all fulness dwell” (Col 1:19).
roots_summary: Greek apaugasma (G541), the effulgence of glory; Greek charakter (G5481), the express image.
roots_lines: Greek apaugasma (G541) — a radiance shining forth from its source; Hebrews 1:3.
Greek charakter (G5481) — an exact impress, the express image; Hebrews 1:3.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, to uphold, to carry along; Hebrews 1:3.
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory, weight of manifested excellence; John 17:5.
Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, all power given; Matthew 28:18.
usage: “upholding all things by the word of his power” (Heb 1:3) — the Giessen position of withheld use.
“the glory which I had with thee before the world was” (Joh 17:5) — the Saxon decision of 1624.
“that in him should all fulness dwell” (Col 1:19) — against the later kenotic theology.

pos: n. (academy and later university of the city of Nuremberg, founded 1575)
etymology: From German Altdorf, the old village, from alt and Dorf.
biblical_def: Altdorf was Nuremberg's own school, founded in 1575 so that the city need not send its sons abroad for the learning its pulpits and its council required, raised to the rank of a university in 1622 and closed in 1809. It was never large or famous, and that is precisely its interest: a middling institution kept for two centuries by one city at its own expense, turning out the ministers, lawyers and schoolmasters a Protestant commonwealth has to have. The dictionary records Altdorf as the type of the thing rather than a great example of it, because the Reformation was carried by hundreds of such schools and remembered through a dozen. Paul's charge to Timothy is addressed to the workman and not to the celebrated: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education in which young persons are instructed in the branches of learning, to study as to fix the mind closely upon a subject, and diligence as steady application and constant effort.
webster_full: SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which young persons are instructed in the several branches of learning.
STUD'Y, v.i. To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to apply the mind to books.
DILIGENCE, n. Steady application in business of any kind; constant effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
PROFESS'OR, n. One who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; particularly, an officer in a university, college or other seminary.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
corruption_summary: Nuremberg's own academy from 1575, a university from 1622, supplying the city's ministers and schoolmasters for two centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern taste for the exceptional, which measures a seminary by its most famous graduate and so cannot see the ordinary work that is the whole point of it. Altdorf produced almost nobody a general reader has heard of, and it supplied a city's pulpits for two hundred years.

The principle to recover is that careful handling of the text is a trade to be learned, and that learning it is a duty laid on the ordinary minister. The charge is to labour at it: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15). Understanding is to be sought as the chief acquisition — “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom” (Pro 4:7) — and the public use of it is specified: “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13). The limit is given too, lest study become its own end: “much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecc 12:12).
roots_summary: Greek spoudazo (G4704), to be diligent; Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight.
roots_lines: Greek spoudazo (G4704) — to make haste, to be diligent, to labour; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, to handle rightly; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek ergates (G2040) — a workman, a labourer at a trade; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom, skill in living; Proverbs 4:7.
Greek anagnosis (G320) — the reading, public recital of Scripture; 1 Timothy 4:13.
usage: “a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — founded 1575 at the city's own expense.
“Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom” (Pro 4:7) — raised to a university in 1622.
“give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) — two hundred years of pulpits supplied.

pos: n. (town on the Weser; seat of a Hessian university from 1621 to 1809)
etymology: From Low German Rinteln, of uncertain sense, perhaps from a word for a cattle ford on the Weser.
biblical_def: Rinteln held a university for a hundred and eighty-eight years and then lost it. Founded in 1621 by the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel out of a dissolved convent, it taught through the worst of the Thirty Years War, changed hands with the territory, kept a modest Reformed and later mixed faculty, and was dissolved by Napoleon's brother in 1809 along with a dozen other small German foundations. Nothing remains of it but a library scattered among larger ones. The dictionary records Rinteln deliberately, as the counterweight to every entry that celebrates an institution: schools, orders, confessional settlements and the cities that house them are all things that are made, and things that are made can be shaken. “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) is not pessimism about building; it is the only ground on which building is worth doing at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a foundation as the groundwork of anything and that upon which anything stands, to build as to construct or erect an edifice, and ruin as that change of a thing which entirely defeats its structure or purpose.
webster_full: FOUNDATION, n. The basis or groundwork of anything; that upon which anything stands.
BUILD, v.t. To construct; to erect, as an edifice.
RUIN, n. [L. ruina, from ruo, to fall.] Destruction; fall; overthrow; that change of any thing which destroys it, or entirely defeats its structure or purpose.
LABOUR, n. Exertion of body or mind for the attainment of some object, especially when severe or continued.
scriptures: A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Mat 7:25
And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
And this word, Yet once more, signifieth the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain.
corruption_summary: A Hessian university founded 1621, dissolved 1809; the entry that answers every celebration of an institution.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is institutional confidence: the assumption that a seminary, a denomination or a confessional settlement will carry the faith forward because it exists, so that maintaining the body is mistaken for keeping the deposit. Rinteln existed for nearly two centuries and is now a footnote.

The principle to recover is that only what God builds stands, and that the one foundation is not an institution at all. The psalm states the condition for every work of building and watching alike: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1). The house that survives the storm is the one founded on rock — “and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock” (Mat 7:25) — and the foundation is a Person: “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11). Everything made is in the end shaken away, “that those things which cannot be shaken may remain” (Heb 12:27).

“For other foundation can no man lay” (1Co 3:11) — a faculty kept through the Thirty Years War.
“that those things which cannot be shaken may remain” (Heb 12:27) — dissolved in 1809, its library scattered.

pos: n. (Saxon town on the Elbe; the Torgau Articles of 1530 and the Torgau Book of 1576)
etymology: From a Slavic root for a market place, torg; German Torgau.
biblical_def: Torgau is a small Saxon town that twice supplied the draft for a confession. In March 1530, before the Diet of Augsburg, Luther, Melanchthon, Bugenhagen and Jonas drew up the Torgau Articles on the abuses of the church, and those articles became the second part of the Augsburg Confession. Forty-six years later, after a generation of quarrelling between the strict Lutherans and the Philippists, a conference at Torgau produced the Torgau Book, which Andreae and the others revised into the Formula of Concord of 1577. The castle chapel at Torgau, consecrated by Luther in 1544, was also the first church building raised specifically for evangelical worship. The dictionary records Torgau because concord of this kind is laborious, documentary and slow, and because Scripture asks for it in exactly those terms: “that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind” (Php 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines concord as agreement between persons and union in opinions and views, an article as a single clause in a system of regulations or other writing, and accord as harmony of mind and concurrence of opinion.
webster_full: CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests.
AR'TICLE, n. A single clause in a contract, account, system of regulations, treaty, or other writing; a particular item.
ACCORD, n. Agreement; harmony of mind; consent; concurrence of opinion.
AGREE'MENT, n. Harmony of opinion, action or character; a compact or bargain.
scriptures: Php 2:2
Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind.
That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.
It seemed good unto us, being assembled with one accord, to send chosen men unto you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
Eph 4:13
Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ:
corruption_summary: The Torgau Articles of 1530, which became part of the Augsburg Confession, and the Torgau Book of 1576 behind the Formula of Concord.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the expectation that unity should be felt rather than written, so that a church pursues concord by avoiding the articles that divide it. Torgau did the opposite twice: it wrote the disputed points down, in order, until both parties could put their names to the same sentences.

The principle to recover is that genuine unity is unity in a stated faith, achieved by labour over words. The apostle asks for an agreement that reaches the mind: “that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind” (Php 2:2). Its pattern and its end are the Son's own prayer: “That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee” (Joh 17:21). The first council reached it by assembly and a written letter — “being assembled with one accord, to send chosen men unto you” (Act 15:25) — and the goal is explicitly doctrinal: “Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God” (Eph 4:13).

pos: n. (Thuringian town below the Wartburg; Luther's schooling, and the castle where he translated the New Testament)
etymology: From German Eisenach, from the Nesse stream and a word for water, aha; Latin Isenacum.
biblical_def: Eisenach holds both ends of Luther's life with the Bible. He went to school in the town from 1498 to 1501, lodging with the Cotta family and singing for his bread; and in May 1521, after the Diet of Worms, he was taken for his safety to the Wartburg on the hill above it, where in eleven weeks of the following winter he translated the New Testament out of Erasmus's Greek into German. That translation, printed at Wittenberg in September 1522, gave the German people the Scriptures in a prose they could read aloud, and fixed the written language itself for four centuries. The dictionary records Eisenach for the plainest of reasons: this is where a hunted man, forbidden to preach, put the word of God into the hands of a nation instead. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8), and the emperor's ban is among the grass.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the Word in theology as the second person in the Trinity, to endure as to last and continue in the same state without perishing, and prophecy as a declaration of something to come.
webster_full: WORD, n. In theology, the second person in the Trinity, called also the Logos.
ENDURE, v.i. To last; to continue in the same state without perishing.
PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come; in Scripture, also a burden or oracle.
TRANSLATE, v.t. To remove from one place or condition to another.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
But the word of the Lord endureth for ever. And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you.
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
corruption_summary: Luther's school town, and the Wartburg above it where he translated the New Testament in the winter of 1521.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the quiet assumption that a vernacular Bible in every house is a settled fact of the furniture rather than something men were hunted for. The Wartburg translation was made by a man under imperial ban, in disguise, in a borrowed room, against the certainty that printing it would be a capital matter for somebody.

The principle to recover is that the word of God outlasts every power that opposes it, and that it is given to be searched. The contrast is absolute: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). Peter applies it directly to the gospel preached: “But the word of the Lord endureth for ever. And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you” (1Pe 1:25). The Lord commands the search and names its object: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39). And the written word is the surer light: “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19).
